parts.spoken_English: Before 1840, British postage was levied according to the number of sheets in a letter and the mileage of its carriage.
The sum was usually payable on delivery, so the person receiving the correspondence, not the sender, settled it.
Prices thus fluctuated from one postal item to the next.
In 1837 Rowland Hill published a booklet urging reform.
Parliament enacted the campaigner's proposal in 1839, and on 10 January 1840 the Uniform Penny Post began.
A letter of up to half an ounce now cost one penny to any destination in Britain, and the fee was prepaid by whoever sent it.
One flat-rate charge replaced variation with simplicity.
The Penny Black, a one-penny denomination, was released on 1 May 1840, its validity starting on 6 May.
Engraved on it was a youthful likeness of Queen Victoria, the reigning monarch.
An aggregate of 68,808,000 were printed.
The sheets had no holes for separation, so each stamp was cut out individually with scissors.
Mailings doubled, from about 80 million items in 1839 to over 169 million in 1840.
The design had a drawback.
Against black, the red cancelling mark was barely noticeable, lacking contrast, and the ink could be erased, leaving stamps vulnerable to reuse.
In February 1841 the Penny Red, cancelled in black ink, arrived to deter tampering and fraud.
As the initiator of postage stamps, Britain set a precedent and earned an exemption.
Its stamps are nameless, with no country inscribed on them.
By international agreement, the sovereign's head suffices for identification, an implicit designation that other countries spell out in print.
